analysis.one_liner: Bans credit card companies from raising interest rates over unrelated debts and requires clearer statements.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop credit card companies from using "universal default" — raising your interest rate because of late payments or problems on other debts, not on that card. It would require statements to show, in plain terms, how many years it would take to pay off your balance if you only make minimum payments. And it would require 30 to 60 days' advance written notice before a company could raise your rate or add a new fee, and bar new fees and rate increases from applying retroactively to balances you already owe.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of households carrying credit card balances. Someone whose rate was hiked because of a late payment on an unrelated bill would keep their original rate. Everyone with a balance would see on each statement how long minimum payments would keep them in debt, and no one could have a rate increase or new fee applied to money they already borrowed without weeks of specific advance notice.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits creditors from raising a card's interest rate based on adverse information — such as the consumer's credit score or information on a credit report — about anything other than that consumer's own account [S2][S3].

Requires each statement to show, in a clear table, the minimum payment in dollars and as a percentage of the balance, and how many months it would take to pay off the full balance making only minimum payments [S2][S3].

Requires 30 days' notice (60 days for most rate increases) before rates rise or new fees take effect, sent separately from the bill, and bars most rate increases from applying to balances already outstanding [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and finance companies — would lose revenue from universal-default rate hikes, retroactive rate increases, and fees imposed without advance notice. To the extent issuers priced risk differently as a result, some borrowers with poor credit could face higher upfront rates instead of surprise increases later.

drawbacks.text: Banning universal default removes one way issuers manage risk across customers; issuers argued such limits could push them to charge higher rates to weaker-credit borrowers up front, shifting costs rather than eliminating them (general industry argument; not in the provided sources).

The disclosure requirement adds compliance costs to issuers, which are generally passed on through fees and rates spread across all cardholders (general mechanism; not quantified in the provided sources).
The bill addresses only disclosure and rate-change practices; it does not cap interest rates or fees, so the underlying cost of card debt would remain whatever issuers choose to charge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections target practices that hit people at their most vulnerable — a rate spike triggered by a mistake on a different bill, or a fee applied to debt already incurred. The main cost falls on a concentrated industry and on accurate pricing of risky borrowers, which is a real trade-off but a modest one next to the consumer protections gained. The bill is narrow: it does not cap rates or fees.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its consumer credit subcommittee, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on July 27, 2005, with 32 Democratic cosponsors including Barney Frank, Carolyn McCarthy, and Barbara Lee among the original cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction [S1][S5].
On August 24, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit — the last recorded action before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card-issuing banks, which kept the ability to raise rates over unrelated debts and change terms with little notice. Similar restrictions eventually passed in a later Congress, after this bill had died.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an independent and all 32 cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-run Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and finance companies)
industries.note: Universal default — raising rates because of a customer's unrelated debts — and applying rate increases to existing balances are direct revenue sources for issuers. The bill bans both and requires advance notice before new fees, directly cutting fee and interest income that comes out of ordinary cardholders' pockets.

The bill bars issuers from using credit report information and credit scores to raise card rates, slightly reducing one use of consumer report data, but leaves the reporting industry's role otherwise intact.
